confidence_why: Steriade 1984, Chitoran 2002, Roca 1999, Franzén and Horne 1997 and Spinu 2026 all place Romanian stress within the last three syllables, lexically variable in position and never on inflectional endings; the only disagreement is whether the default position follows syllable weight (Steriade 1984) or morphological structure with no weight effect (Chitoran 2002, Roca 1999), which the record already hedges.

sweep_summary: Five title hits for Romanian. Two are about word stress: Roca 1999 (Eurotyp chapter; paywalled at De Gruyter, WAF-blocked; the catalog already carries its StressTyp2 excerpt 1717) and Iscrulescu 2006 (Benjamins, closed; abstract obtained via OpenAlex and saved). The Iscrulescu abstract explicitly argues that Romanian nominal stress is weight-insensitive (syllabic trochees, final-consonant final stress as opacity), contra Steriade 1984's weight-sensitive analysis, so it contradicts the mechanism behind the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding at the analysis level; the full paper is high priority. Ulivi 1985 (secondary stress in Daco-Romanian dialects, RRL) is print-only (lingv.ro archive starts 2006) and concerns secondary stress. Göbbel 2003 and Swerts 2007 are sentence-level prosody (focus/pitch accent), not word stress; Swerts's TLDR ('accent distribution.. demarcative rather than contrastive' in Romanian) was recorded. Iscrulescu's ROA 887 dissertation was downloaded and checked: no stress-placement statement. No new first-hand statement supersedes Steriade 1984. DuckDuckGo/Bing/Google/HathiTrust/Internet Archive were unreachable or could not be reached by automated download, so discovery relied on Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, ROA and publisher/journal sites.

new_statements.quote: The acoustic properties of two types of prosodic prominence, stress and focus at the lexical and sentence levels, respectively, are examined in Romanian. Real three-syllable words were produced by 9 native speakers in two sentential contexts [...]. The position of stress was systematically varied, so it appeared on each of the three syllable positions. Analyses of over 3,500 vowels show that duration and F0 are robust correlates of lexical stress in Romanian, consistent with cross-linguistic patterns.

Reading: the abstract states that stress in real trisyllabic words was placed on each of the three syllable positions and that duration and F0 cue 'lexical stress'; it states no placement rule. Note that 'lexical' there contrasts with sentence-level focus (word-level stress), not 'lexically specified', so the lexical (unpredictable) label rests on the three-position fact together with the catalog's WALS 14A 'No fixed stress', which is a fair use of the fixed list. new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's WALS-based 'lexical stress' / 'no fixed stress' entry and with the StressTyp2 U/P (final-if-heavy, else penult) rule only as a lexical system; it adds that antepenultimate stress occurs in real trisyllabic words (beyond WALS 15A 'ultimate or penultimate') and that duration and F0 are the acoustic cues, focus enhancing them additively. Not a placement source; the catalog rule field for this record is empty.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The abstract treats Romanian stress as lexical (word-level) stress whose position is not fixed: in real trisyllabic words it can sit on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, and its acoustic correlates are duration and F0 (with slightly more peripheral vowels). No placement rule is stated in the abstract; the full text (CC-BY, but behind the degruyterbrill.com WAF: automated download 202/empty twice, direct download 405, no archived copy at the Internet Archive, no repository copy) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern standard (Daco-)Romanian; Klein 2007 also treats Siswati (ssw), a Bantu language, in its second half, with no tone or stress statement for it.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Romanian word stress is treated as lexical: in real trisyllabic words stress can fall on the antepenult, the penult or the final syllable (all three positions are attested and were used as stimuli); stressed vowels are longer and higher in F0, and sentence focus enhances these cues additively. The abstract states no placement rule or default.

It is thought that Daco-Romanian has free dynamic stress (meaning that stress is largely unpredictable and entirely lexical) like most Romance languages, except French [...] [p. 92] Intonation languages with lexical stress do not assign tones at the word level (Féry 2017). Amsterdam: John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/cilt.306.04man [open author postprint: Purdue e-Pubs, School of Languages and Cultures Faculty Publications 14]
tone_statements.quote: This experiment describes the phonetic make up of broad focus and contrastive focus declarative sentences in Romanian. In broad focus sentences, speakers of Romanian consistently place a pitch accent on each syllable with lexical stress. The pitch range of these accents is progressively lower towards the end of the sentence and the peaks of the pre-nuclear accents align with the post-tonic syllable. … In contrastive focus declarative sentences, speakers use several strategies based on pitch range, pitch alignment and duration to make the accented word more prominent than the rest.
tone_statements.locator: postprint p. 12, sec. 4 'Discussion and conclusions', first two paragraphs (heading at foot of p. 11)
tone_statements.summary: Intonation study: pitch is post-lexical; in declaratives every lexically stressed syllable carries an intonational pitch accent whose shape and range mark focus. No lexical tone is described.

sources.citation: Buja, Elena. 2024. The acquisition of diphthongs by Romanian-speaking children. Bulletin of the Transilvania University of Brasov, Series IV: Philology and Cultural Studies 17(66)(2): 49-70. doi:10.31926/but.pcs.2024.66.17.2.4
sources.quote: Unlike the full vowels, which could form syllable nuclei and carry stress, the semivowels cannot [...] According to Rosetti (1986, 94), Romanian diphthongs take the stress on the most open vocalic element (a'i, a'u ea', ia', e'u etc.). [...] The diphthong /ĕa/ occurs in stressed syllables ('pleacă /'plĕa.kə/ 'leave!) or in word-final position ('cartea /'kar.tĕa 'the.book'), and very rarely in unstressed syllables in word-mid position (dumneata /dum.nĕa.'ta/ 'polite form of you (sg.)'). As far as the diphthong /ŏa/ is concerned, this can be found only in stressed contexts: roagă /'rŏa.gə/ 'he prays/begs/asks', foarte /'fŏar.te/ 'very'.
sources.note: marginal: Longitudinal child-acquisition study of Romanian diphthongs that treats syllable stress as one factor in acquisition; stress is a variable, not the object.

sources.citation: Herce, Borja & Pricop, Bogdan. 2024. VeLeRo: an inflected verbal lexicon of standard Romanian and a quantitative analysis of morphological predictability. Language Resources and Evaluation 59: 621-637 [issue dated 2025; published online 23 March 2024]. doi:10.1007/s10579-024-09721-3
sources.quote: In Romanian, stress can be oxytonic (final syllable), paroxytonic (penultimate syllable) or proparoxitonic (antepenultimate syllable) and is not marked orthographicaly. Some authors (Chitoran, 1996) have claimed that stress is highly predictable, depending, among others, on the part of speech of the lexical item, but some others (Dindelegan & Maiden, 2013), have claimed that stress is largely unpredictable and highly mobile, especially in verbal inflections. RoMorphoDict was used as the point of departure for building the present resource because it indicates stress consistently on polysyllabic verbs. For consistency (i.e. to avoid spurious morphological contrasts), we added stress markers on monosyllabic verb forms as well (on the only vowel when a word had only one, or on the most open vowel in case the word contained a diphthong or triphthong).
sources.note: marginal: Presents a phonologically transcribed lexicon of 7,297 Romanian verb paradigms and explains how stress, diphthongs/hiatus and palatalization were handled in phonemization; the object is morphological predictability, not stress.

sources.quote: This experiment describes the phonetic make up of broad focus and contrastive focus declarative sentences in Romanian. In broad focus sentences, speakers of Romanian consistently place a pitch accent on each syllable with lexical stress. The pitch range of these accents is progressively lower towards the end of the sentence and the peaks of the pre-nuclear accents align with the post-tonic syllable. … In contrastive focus declarative sentences, speakers use several strategies based on pitch range, pitch alignment and duration to make the accented word more prominent than the rest.
